An example is the M 7.8 1939 Chillán intermediate-depth earthquake6, which tragically led to a larger loss of life in Chile than any of the megathrust events on record. reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:

Jia et al. investigate the rupture characteristics of the large, intermediate-depth Calama earthquake, finding that it had a steeply dipping fault plane extending ~75 km down from the hypocenter. By themselves, the combined analyses are rigorous and convincing, making this event one of the best constrained intermediate depth earthquakes of this magnitude I have read about. But what makes the earthquake potentially compelling for publication in Nature Communications is its context within the thermal conditions of the slab. As the authors explain well, the rupture propagated from the cold core of the slab, where earthquakes are known to occur, out into the hotter regions of the slab where brittle, elastic-rebound processes are unexpected. In my opinion, the manuscript is convincing and in good shape, other than some minor comments, provided below.
What I find myself wondering about is the thermal modeling and relationship between the Calama earthquake and temperature. [Full disclosure, I am not an expert in intermediate depth earthquakes or in the thermal state of the Nazca slab.] Fig. 5 of the manuscript shows that this section of the Nazca slab has substantially more earthquakes along the deeper cold-to-hot transition in the subducting slab than the other three settings shown. I have not looked closely at other subduction zones to see if this uniqueness extends globally, but I think this is something to probe further about the setting of the Calama earthquake since it is essential to the argument about rupture process. Could it be that the slab in the Calama region is actually slightly deeper than currently proposed, so these events (and the 2024 rupture) are still mostly within the cold slab core? Or do the authors know of alternative interpretations for the number of deeper intermediate earthquakes along the base of the slab here? Addressing this would go a long way towards solidifying the interpretive aspects of this study.
Minor Comments:
An aspect of this problem the authors allude to but never address directly is the topic of strain rates. How it relates to the brittle-ductile transition is implicit in the rupture mechanisms for intermediate-depth earthquakes, but I would like to see it laid out more explicitly (cf., ll. 55-56). One thing in particular that strikes me is that at typical strain rates and temperatures of ~1000ºC, even with a mechanism like thermal runaway to localize strain it is hard to imagine having enough elastic strain energy stored for an earthquake. I understand that this is one of the key points in the manuscript. I think it would be helpful to lay it out for the reader.
I am aware of several other thermal models for subducting slabs. Qualitatively, the results here look similar, but obviously the details matter for interpreting this event. It would be good to have a comparison (even a brief one) and some references to those other models (e.g., somewhere in ll. 198-205)
Detailed Comments:
ll. 26-34: I think it would be better to disentangle observations and analyses from interpretations about rupture mechanisms here, focusing first on the detailed aspects of the event, then the comparison to thermal models, and finally the connection to dehydration embrittlement or shear thermal instability
l. 42: What is the point the authors are trying to make in saying that “the number of earthquakes drops markedly from shallow to deep”? Could this statement be removed?
ll. 57-58: The references for these intermediate earthquake processes are helpful, but it might also be useful to give a brief (one sentence) description of each process too
l. 60: What exactly do the authors mean by “environmental conditions”? Temperature? Other properties?
ll. 59-62: How would knowing things like rupture extent contribute to constraining the process? Making this explicit will help guide the reader through the rest of the manuscript.
ll. 67-68: For an M 7.8, a few tens of km is not that far away. What is the location quality of the 1950 event?
l. 68: I think there is no need for “However” at the beginning of this sentence.
l. 69: I am unsure about what “constrained only by analog teleseismic data” implies. That it only has a focal mechanism or moment tensor?
l. 69: I think it would be good to put a period after “indicating a normal faulting earthquake” and then talk about the 2005 earthquake separately. I initially thought the points were connected, but they are not. Also, just a point to note: the concept of “normal faulting” is a little different for intermediate depth earthquakes, since the slab is dipping and surrounded by rocks (i.e., there is not a requirement for a principal stress axis to be perpendicular to a free surface).
ll. 85-88: I would divide this sentence into two, one describing the information obtained from seismic data and the other describing the information obtained from co-seismic displacements
l. 90: Maybe I missed it, but I do not think the “core of the slab” has been defined yet
ll. 96ff: I find the description of these results really clear and easy to follow
ll. 135ff: I think some references might be useful here (e.g., for EGF approaches, the stretching of the source duration caused by horizontal rupture, or the linearity of the rupture dimension/velocity)
ll. 153-154: I confused “coherent phases” with seismic phases at first. Is there a better word here?
l. 157: Some numbers would be helpful here: How many pulses? What size asperities?
ll. 174ff: I would make the geodetic analysis its own paragraph. Also, just a comment that at this depth I suspect that it is challenging to resolve a slip distribution, much like it is challenging to resolve fault geometry.

ll. 193-197: I am unsure of the argument being made about aftershocks and temperature here. Sorry my comment is not more helpful.

I know this has been argued for the region further north (where the 2005 Tarapaca occurred), but I am unaware of a similar argument here. Also, in very large megathrust earthquakes, these stresses are recovered, so it might not be a long-term effect. I guess my point is that I am unsure about whether high coupling is a “key factor” or not.

1. In this work, the spatiotempral rupture process of the 2024 Calama earthquake is investigated with a subevent inversion instead of a Finite Fault Inversion (FFI). Please give a explanation for chosing subevent inversion instead of FFI, since most rupture process model are built with FFI method.
Response: We agree that Finite Fault Inversion (FFI) is a powerful and widely used technique for imaging detailed rupture processes. However, for our investigation of the 2024 Calama earthquake, we choose subevent modeling approach due to its advantages in cases with notable unknowns, which we believe leads to a more robust and reliable primary model of the source. Our rationale is based on the following points:
First, fewer assumptions on fault geometry. FFI requires defining a specific fault plane with fixed strike and dip, which can bias results if the true geometry is uncertain, as is often the case early in an event like the Calama earthquake. The subevent model avoids this by not requiring a predefined fault, which allows us to image rupture without imposing a possibly incorrect fault geometry.
Second, objective imaging of the rupture evolution. The subevent approach lets the data drive the reconstruction of rupture progression without enforcing assumptions about rupture velocity or direction. On the other hand, FFI is more constrained by model assumptions on rupture spatiotemporal evolution.
Finally, improved inversion robustness. FFI involves hundreds to thousands of unknown parameters (e.g., slip, rake, rise time on subfaults) in the inversion, which can make the inversion unstable or non-unique, especially with limited seismic data coverage. On the other hand, the subevent model has much fewer nonlinear parameters (25 for the 5-subevent inversion), making it more robust and less prone to overfitting.
Thus, for the 2024 Calama earthquake, we prioritized reliability and interpretability by using the subevent method to reduce assumptions and generate a robust first-order view of rupture evolution.
We briefly addressed this point in L438-441.
2. As for determining rupture speed of the rupture, the authors conducted directivity analysis instead of Back Projection method, please give a explanation for this.
Response: Our primary objective here was to constrain the down-dip rupture characteristics, including directivity and rupture speed. Resolving vertical directivity fundamentally relies on observing the Doppler effect from a wide geometric range of stations, and specifically by contrasting the apparent source durations of downgoing waves (recorded at teleseismic distances) and upgoing waves (recorded at local or regional distances). For this reason, we chose the subevent modeling which provides the depth-wise flexibility and resolution of the rupture process, as well as the directivity analysis based on the deconvolution and comparison of downgoing and upgoing apparent source time functions (aSTFs). These methods allowed us to quantify the Doppler-like shortening and lengthening caused by rupture propagation. The systematic variation in STF duration as a function of station azimuth and takeoff angle was further modeled to provide a robust estimate of the rupture speed in the down-dip direction.
The Back Projection (BP) method, which typically uses only high-frequency P-waves from teleseismic arrays, is an excellent tool for tracking the horizontal migration of high-frequency energy release. However, its reliance on a narrow cone of downgoing teleseismic waves makes it geometrically insensitive to rupture propagation along the dip of the fault. It cannot effectively distinguish between a shallow and a deep source of radiation within its time window, and hence it cannot resolve vertical directivity or the down-dip rupture speed.
We briefly addressed this point in L441-443.

This allowed comparison with an established, representative standard.
The overall source durations and rupture parameters derived from these automatically truncated STFs were qualitatively similar to those from our preferred selections. However, we found that the rigid 25% threshold introduced significant unnatural truncations and artifacts, particularly for the teleseismic P-wave STFs where complex wave propagation can distort signal shape. This confirms our results’ robustness while highlighting that our selection offers a more physically meaningful measure for the source durations.

1. In this work, the spatiotempral rupture process of the 2024 Calama earthquake is investigated with a subevent inversion instead of a Finite Fault Inversion (FFI). Please give a explanation for chosing subevent inversion instead of FFI, since most rupture process model are built with FFI method.
Response: We agree that Finite Fault Inversion (FFI) is a powerful and widely used technique for imaging detailed rupture processes. However, for our investigation of the 2024 Calama earthquake, we choose subevent modeling approach due to its advantages in cases with notable unknowns, which we believe leads to a more robust and reliable primary model of the source. Our rationale is based on the following points:
First, fewer assumptions on fault geometry. FFI requires defining a specific fault plane with fixed strike and dip, which can bias results if the true geometry is uncertain, as is often the case early in an event like the Calama earthquake. The subevent model avoids this by not requiring a predefined fault, which allows us to image rupture without imposing a possibly incorrect fault geometry.
Second, objective imaging of the rupture evolution. The subevent approach lets the data drive the reconstruction of rupture progression without enforcing assumptions about rupture velocity or direction. On the other hand, FFI is more constrained by model assumptions on rupture spatiotemporal evolution.
Finally, improved inversion robustness. FFI involves hundreds to thousands of unknown parameters (e.g., slip, rake, rise time on subfaults) in the inversion, which can make the inversion unstable or non-unique, especially with limited seismic data coverage. On the other hand, the subevent model has much fewer nonlinear parameters (25 for the 5-subevent inversion), making it more robust and less prone to overfitting.
Thus, for the 2024 Calama earthquake, we prioritized reliability and interpretability by using the subevent method to reduce assumptions and generate a robust first-order view of rupture evolution.
We briefly addressed this point in L438-441.
2. As for determining rupture speed of the rupture, the authors conducted directivity analysis instead of Back Projection method, please give a explanation for this.

For this reason, we chose the subevent modeling which provides the depth-wise flexibility and resolution of the rupture process, as well as the directivity analysis based on the deconvolution and comparison of downgoing and upgoing apparent source time functions (aSTFs). These methods allowed us to quantify the Doppler-like shortening and lengthening caused by rupture propagation. The systematic variation in STF duration as a function of station azimuth and takeoff angle was further modeled to provide a robust estimate of the rupture speed in the down-dip direction.
The Back Projection (BP) method, which typically uses only high-frequency P-waves from teleseismic arrays, is an excellent tool for tracking the horizontal migration of high-frequency energy release. However, its reliance on a narrow cone of downgoing teleseismic waves makes it geometrically insensitive to rupture propagation along the dip of the fault. It cannot effectively distinguish between a shallow and a deep source of radiation within its time window, and hence it cannot resolve vertical directivity or the down-dip rupture speed.
We briefly addressed this point in L441-443.

This effect is compounded by the limited sensitivity of our long-period data to certain parameters; for durations longer than ~5 seconds, varying the duration has a minimal impact on the waveform fit, creating trade-offs with other parameters and leading to the wide, skewed posteriors shown.

Response: We agree that understanding how significant elastic strain energy can be stored and released seismically at temperatures approaching 1000°C is important to understanding intermediate and deep earthquakes, and a clearer explanation will benefit the reader.
The key is the strong dependence of a material's deformation style on the rate of applied strain. At low strain rate, the slab movement provides the loading and steadily increases the elastic strain. The materials at these temperatures will eventually deform ductilely over geological timescales through processes like dislocation creep. However, mechanisms like the dehydration embrittlement and transformational faulting of metastable olivine can trigger intermediate-depth and deep earthquake ruptures, respectively, which are localized high-strain-rate phenomena, where shear thermal runaway can be initiated. This localization creates a positive feedback loop: localized shear deformation generates heat faster than it can diffuse away, which dramatically weakens the rock (reducing its viscosity) within a narrow zone. This weakening further concentrates the strain, leading to even faster heating and runaway instability that culminates in a rapid and large-scale rupture, both for intermediate-depth and deep focus events.

However, for our investigation of the 2024 Calama earthquake, we choose subevent modeling approach due to its advantages in cases with notable unknowns, which we believe leads to a more robust and reliable primary model of the source. Our rationale is based on the following points:
First, fewer assumptions on fault geometry. FFI requires defining a specific fault plane with fixed strike and dip, which can bias results if the true geometry is uncertain, as is often the case early in an event like the Calama earthquake. The subevent model avoids this by not requiring a predefined fault, which allows us to image rupture without imposing a possibly incorrect fault geometry.
Second, objective imaging of the rupture evolution. The subevent approach lets the data drive the reconstruction of rupture progression without enforcing assumptions about rupture velocity or direction. On the other hand, FFI is more constrained by model assumptions on rupture spatiotemporal evolution.
Finally, improved inversion robustness. FFI involves hundreds to thousands of unknown parameters (e.g., slip, rake, rise time on subfaults) in the inversion, which can make the inversion unstable or non-unique, especially with limited seismic data coverage. On the other hand, the subevent model has much fewer nonlinear parameters (25 for the 5-subevent inversion), making it more robust and less prone to overfitting.

Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s concern regarding potential uncertainties in the slab geometry. The Nazca slab geometry used in our thermal modeling is not arbitrary–it is constrained by multiple independent datasets, including regional seismic tomography and the distribution of hundreds of thousands of relocated earthquakes that collectively delineate the shape of the slab interface. In fact, the seismicity pattern itself provides one of the most reliable indicators of slab location.
To make it more clear, we have updated Figure 5 (and the supplementary Figure S11) with the latest high-resolution relocated catalog from the Centro Sismológico Nacional (CSN) of Chile. As shown in revised Supplementary Figure S11, even when adopting an alternative geometry (e.g., from the Slab2 model) and varying the slab age (which changes the effective thickness of the cold core), the along-dip rupture of the Calama earthquake should still extend beyond the serpentinite dehydration isotherm. The apparent 'smearing' of this seismicity could partly reflect inherent hypocentral uncertainties. An aspect of this problem the authors allude to but never address directly is the topic of strain rates. How it relates to the brittle-ductile transition is implicit in the rupture mechanisms for intermediate-depth earthquakes, but I would like to see it laid out more explicitly (cf., ll. 55-56). One thing in particular that strikes me is that at typical strain rates and temperatures of ~1000ºC, even with a mechanism like thermal runaway to localize strain it is hard to imagine having enough elastic strain energy stored for an earthquake. I understand that this is one of the key points in the manuscript. I think it would be helpful to lay it out for the reader.
Response: We agree that understanding how significant elastic strain energy can be stored and released seismically at temperatures approaching 1000°C is important to understanding intermediate and deep earthquakes, and a clearer explanation will benefit the reader.
The key is the strong dependence of a material's deformation style on the rate of applied strain. At low strain rate, the slab movement provides the loading and steadily increases the elastic strain. The materials at these temperatures will eventually deform ductilely over geological timescales through processes like dislocation creep. However, mechanisms like the dehydration embrittlement and transformational faulting of metastable olivine can trigger intermediate-depth and deep earthquake ruptures, respectively, which are localized high-strain-rate phenomena, where shear thermal runaway can be initiated. This localization creates a positive feedback loop: localized shear deformation generates heat faster than it can diffuse away, which dramatically weakens the rock (reducing its viscosity) within a narrow zone. This weakening further concentrates the strain, leading to even faster heating and runaway instability that culminates in a rapid and large-scale rupture, both for intermediate-depth and deep focus events.
We added discussions in L253-285 to address this point.

This means that all these independent thermal models will support our conclusion that the rupture extends beyond the 650 degree isotherm of the serpentinite dehydration and transitioned to thermal runaway.
